channel.title: Transcription on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Transcription on Best of AI

item.title: Webex
item.description:
Webex is one of the older names in video conferencing, and Cisco has kept it competitive by adding hardware, calling, and collaboration tools. Companies use it for meetings, webinars, team messaging, a phone system, and conference room devices, with security and compliance controls that suit regulated industries and government.

The AI Assistant adds help across these pieces. It writes meeting summaries and action items, answers questions about what was discussed, catches up people who join late, and summarizes long message threads. Audio features remove background noise and can isolate a speaker’s voice in a loud room, and real-time translation and captions help international teams. Cisco also sells AI agents for contact centers.

item.title: MAI-Voice-2.1
item.description: Microsoft released MAI-Voice-2.1 and a low-latency MAI-Voice-2.1-Flash on October 1, 2026, alongside MAI-Transcribe-2-Streaming, which transcribes live speech in 60 languages with partial results in just over 100 ms.

item.title: Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe
item.description: Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe follows instructions for transcription, translation, and speaker attribution across 40 languages, and handles recordings up to an hour long.

item.title: Nemotron 3 Diarization
item.description: NVIDIA released Nemotron 3 Diarization on September 23, 2026, a 100-million-parameter open-weight model that tracks up to eight overlapping speakers in real-time streaming audio. It targets call-center and meeting-transcription pipelines that need to know who said what as the audio comes in, rather than after the fact.

item.title: MosMos
item.description:
MosMos is a dictation and meeting tool for Mac. A user speaks and text appears in the active app, formatted to fit the context: casual in a chat, structured in a document, code-friendly in an editor. A personal glossary learns names and technical terms, reducing repeated mistakes.

In meetings, MosMos can record and transcribe with labels for each speaker and produce notes and action items afterward. Combining dictation and meeting features in one app saves switching between tools.

item.title: Whisper
item.description:
Whisper is a speech-to-text model trained on a very large and varied collection of multilingual audio. That training made it unusually robust: it copes with accents, background noise, and technical vocabulary better than many earlier systems, and it works across dozens of languages. It also detects the spoken language automatically, adds punctuation, and can translate speech from other languages into English text.

The model is released as open source with several sizes, from small ones that run on a laptop to large ones that need a good GPU. That openness led to a wide ecosystem: faster versions such as whisper.cpp and faster-whisper, tools that add timestamps and speaker labels, and many apps for transcription, subtitles, and dictation that use it behind the scenes. OpenAI also offers it through its API for people who do not want to host it.

item.title: Laxis
item.description:
Laxis joins online meetings, records and transcribes them, and produces summaries with action items and key points. Sales teams use it to log call notes in the CRM automatically, and researchers and recruiters use it for interviews. Search across past meetings helps find specific topics.

Extra features include templates for different meeting types, follow-up email drafts, and analytics on conversations. Integrations connect with Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, and CRMs such as Salesforce and HubSpot.

item.title: Rewatch
item.description:
Rewatch is built on the idea that useful knowledge is trapped in recordings no one rewatches. It captures meetings and async videos, transcribes them, and organizes them into channels and playlists, so employees can find the moment they need by searching words said.

Features include summaries, chapters, comments on moments in the video, and integrations with Zoom, Slack, and calendars. The goal is to let people catch up on meetings quickly and reduce the number of live sessions.

item.title: Avoma
item.description: Avoma joins sales, customer success, and recruiting meetings on Zoom, Google Meet, and Teams, then records and transcribes them and produces notes organized by meeting type. Instead of a generic summary, it uses templates suited to the call, such as a discovery call or a customer check-in, and pulls out action items, objections, and next steps. Notes and key fields can be pushed into CRMs like Salesforce and HubSpot, which saves reps from doing data entry after every call.

item.title: Claap
item.description: Claap targets teams that want fewer live meetings. You can record your screen and camera as a short video, share a link, and let colleagues watch and respond on their own time. The same tool records live calls on Zoom, Google Meet, and Teams, then stores them with a transcript. Comments and reactions can be attached to specific moments, so feedback stays tied to the part of the video it refers to.

item.title: Fathom
item.description: Fathom is known for making meeting notes free. It joins your Zoom, Google Meet, or Microsoft Teams calls, records them, and creates a transcript in real time. You can highlight important moments during the call with a click, and within seconds of the meeting ending, it produces a summary with decisions, action items, and key points that you can share. The free plan includes unlimited recordings and transcripts, which set it apart from competitors that cap free use.

item.title: Fellow
item.description:
Fellow helps teams run better meetings. Before a meeting, it provides shared agendas and templates for one-on-ones, team meetings, and client calls. During the meeting, an AI notetaker records and transcribes, capturing decisions and action items automatically. Afterward, summaries and tasks are sent to attendees.

The platform keeps a record of conversations over time, which suits managers who run recurring one-on-ones. Integrations connect with calendars, Slack, Zoom, Teams, and project tools. AI features answer questions across past meetings and draft follow-up messages. Feedback tools support regular check-ins and performance conversations.

item.title: Fireflies.ai
item.description: Fireflies sends a bot into your meetings, usually named Fred, that records the call and creates a transcript with speaker labels. After the meeting, it produces a summary with action items and key topics, and posts them where your team works. Every meeting becomes searchable text, so you can find what a customer said last month or when a decision was made. It supports dozens of languages and works with the main video call platforms and uploaded recordings.

item.title: Grain
item.description:
Grain records meetings on Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, and other platforms and turns them into transcripts, summaries, and short clips. Its clip feature is a distinguishing idea: instead of sharing a whole recording, you highlight a moment, such as a customer’s feedback or a question about pricing, and share just that clip with colleagues. This makes customer insights easier to spread across product, marketing, and leadership.

AI features produce structured notes from each meeting using templates, such as discovery calls or customer interviews, and answer questions across a library of recordings. Integrations send notes and fields to Salesforce, HubSpot, Notion, and Slack, which cuts manual updates. A desktop capture option can record meetings without a visible bot joining the call, which some teams prefer for external meetings.

item.title: Happy Scribe
item.description:
Happy Scribe converts speech into text. You upload an audio or video file, or connect a source like Zoom or YouTube, and receive a transcript in minutes with speaker labels and timestamps. It supports many languages and dialects, which suits journalists, researchers, podcasters, and companies that work in several markets. A browser editor lets you listen while you correct the text.

Subtitling is a major use. The service can generate subtitles and captions for videos, translate them into other languages, and export in standard formats for YouTube, Vimeo, and video editors. For cases where accuracy matters more, such as legal or broadcast work, you can order human-made transcripts and subtitles, which cost more and take longer. An API and integrations connect it to workflows.

item.title: MeetGeek
item.description:
MeetGeek joins your calendar’s online meetings, records them, and produces a transcript and summary after each one. The summary lists decisions, action items, and key points, and highlights flag important moments. Notes are sent automatically to attendees or to tools like Slack, Notion, HubSpot, and Google Docs, which cuts down on manual write-ups.

Beyond a single meeting, it organizes knowledge across your calls. Hubs group meetings by team or topic, and you can search past conversations or ask questions about them. Meeting templates tailor summaries for sales calls, interviews, or team check-ins, and analytics show participation and talk time. Teams can get insights into patterns across customer calls.

item.title: Notta
item.description: Notta turns speech into text for people who sit through many conversations. You can record in the mobile or web app, upload audio and video files, or let its assistant join Zoom, Google Meet, and Teams calls. The transcript appears in the app with speaker labels and timestamps, and you can search it, edit it, and share it. It supports a large number of languages, which suits international teams, journalists, and researchers.

item.title: Noty.ai
item.description:
Noty.ai is a lightweight tool for people who want meeting notes without much setup. It records and transcribes online meetings, then creates a summary that highlights the main discussion points, decisions, and tasks. The goal is to let participants focus on the conversation instead of typing, and to give everyone a shared record afterward.

Its integrations make the notes easy to reuse. Summaries can be pushed to Notion and other workspace tools, and the transcript is searchable, so you can find what was said about a topic in a past meeting. A browser extension handles recording in Google Meet and Zoom, and a free plan lets individuals try the product.

item.title: Otter.ai
item.description: Otter was one of the first widely used meeting transcription tools. You connect your calendar, and its assistant joins your Zoom, Google Meet, or Teams calls to record, transcribe, and label speakers. The transcript is available live, so participants can follow along, and afterward you get a summary, key points, and action items. Everything is searchable, so you can find what was said in a past meeting by keyword. It also works on phones for in-person conversations and lectures.

item.title: Otter.ai
item.description:
Otter.ai joins online meetings, transcribes the conversation as it happens, and produces notes people can search and share. Speakers are labeled, key points are summarized, and action items are pulled out, so attendees can focus on the discussion instead of taking notes.

Features include an assistant that can answer questions about a meeting or across past meetings, automatic sharing of notes with attendees, and integrations with calendars and collaboration tools. Mobile and web apps handle in-person conversations, lectures, and interviews.

item.title: Rev
item.description:
Rev started as a human transcription marketplace and added automatic transcription as speech recognition improved. Users upload audio or video, and receive a transcript within minutes from the AI service, or within hours from human transcribers who deliver higher accuracy. The choice lets you trade cost and speed for precision, which matters for legal proceedings, journalism, and broadcast captions.

Beyond transcripts, Rev offers captions and subtitles in many languages, translation, and a web editor for correcting and exporting text. Meeting tools record calls and produce notes, and an API supports developers who want to add transcription to products. Accessibility compliance is a big use, because captions help meet legal requirements for education and media.

item.title: Sembly AI
item.description:
Sembly joins your online meetings, records them, and produces a transcript with a structured summary. The summary highlights the main points, tasks, decisions, and risks mentioned, so teams can see what needs follow-up without rewatching. It also supports in-person meetings through its mobile app and uploads of audio files, and works in many languages.

Beyond single meetings, Sembly helps organize knowledge. Workspaces and meeting libraries let teams search past conversations and ask questions across them, and templates adjust the notes for different meeting types such as sales calls or interviews. Integrations push summaries and tasks into Slack, Notion, Asana, Jira, HubSpot, and other tools. Analytics track patterns like meeting time and topics.

item.title: Sonix
item.description:
Sonix focuses on fast, accurate machine transcription with a polished editor. You upload a file or connect a source, and get a transcript with timestamps and speaker labels, which you can edit while listening and the text highlights as the audio plays. It supports over forty languages and can translate transcripts into many more. Journalists, researchers, podcasters, and video producers use it to turn recordings into searchable text.

Additional tools support publishing. Sonix exports subtitles and captions in standard formats, offers a media player that embeds the transcript, and provides search across all your files. Integrations and an API connect it with video editors like Premiere Pro and Final Cut, and Zoom. Teams can share folders and custom vocabulary to improve accuracy on specialized terms.

item.title: SubtitleBee
item.description:
SubtitleBee automates subtitles. You upload a video, choose the spoken language, and the tool transcribes it and creates timed captions, which you can edit in a simple editor. It supports many languages and can translate subtitles into others, helping creators reach international audiences. Typical users are YouTubers, social media managers, educators, and marketers, who need captions because many viewers watch with the sound off.

Style options let captions fit a brand: you can change fonts, colors, positions, and highlight words as they are spoken, which is a popular look on short-form video. Subtitles can be exported as files for use in other editors or burned into the video itself. Plans are tied to the amount of video processed, and the product is in a crowded category.

item.title: Supernormal
item.description:
Supernormal aims to make meeting notes require no effort. A bot joins your scheduled meetings, records and transcribes them, and creates notes organized by templates for different types of meetings, such as sales calls, interviews, one-on-ones, and standups. The notes list decisions, action items, and key points, and are shared with attendees or saved to the tools your team uses.

The product works across platforms, including Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams, and also supports in-person meetings. Integrations push notes to Slack, Notion, HubSpot, Salesforce, and Google Docs. Search and chat features let you look back at past meetings and ask questions, and customization options allow you to adjust the format of the notes.

item.title: Tactiq
item.description:
Tactiq takes a lightweight approach to meeting notes. Instead of sending a recording bot into the call, it runs as a browser extension that captures the meeting’s captions and audio on your device. A live transcript appears in a sidebar as people speak, and you can highlight key moments as the meeting happens. That makes it less intrusive in calls where an unfamiliar bot would raise eyebrows.

After the meeting, AI features produce summaries, action items, and custom outputs from prompts, such as a follow-up email or a status update. The transcript is saved in your account and can be exported to tools like Notion, Google Docs, Slack, and HubSpot. Templates adapt the output for different meeting types, and a search function finds past conversations.

item.title: tl;dv
item.description:
tl;dv, short for “too long; didn’t view,” saves people from rewatching meetings. A bot joins your calls to record and transcribe them in many languages, and you can mark highlights during the call. Afterward, the recording is available with an AI-generated summary and a list of action items, plus timestamps so you can jump to the part that matters. Clips can be shared with people who missed the meeting.

The tool is popular with sales and product teams. It can fill in CRM fields in tools like HubSpot and Salesforce, produce reports across many meetings to spot patterns such as customer objections, and send notes to Slack and Notion. Templates tailor summaries to sales calls, user interviews, and team meetings, and search lets you find topics across your library.

item.title: Gladia
item.description:
Gladia provides speech-to-text as a service for developers. Companies send audio from calls, meetings, or videos and receive transcripts with timestamps, speaker labels, and optional translation. It handles dozens of languages and can detect which one is being spoken.

Real-time transcription suits live captioning and voice agents, while batch processing handles recordings at scale. Extra features include summaries, sentiment, and named entity detection. The API is aimed at products built on audio, such as meeting assistants, call analytics, and media tools.

item.title: Speechmatics
item.description:
Speechmatics provides speech-to-text as a service. Developers send audio and get transcripts with timestamps, speaker labels, and language detection. The company emphasizes accuracy across accents and dialects, which is an area where many systems show bias.

Products include real-time transcription for live captioning and voice agents, batch processing, translation, and deployment options on premises for sensitive data. Customers include media, contact center, and healthcare companies.

Speechmatics is priced by usage. Alternatives include Deepgram, AssemblyAI, OpenAI Whisper, Gladia, and Google Cloud Speech-to-Text. Speechmatics suits organizations needing accurate multilingual transcription.

item.title: Submagic
item.description:
Submagic speeds up editing of talking-head clips. A creator uploads a video, the tool transcribes speech, adds styled captions that highlight words as they are spoken, and suggests emojis, sound effects, and B-roll to keep viewers engaged.

Templates provide the caption looks seen on popular social videos, and users can edit text, timing, and style. Tools for trimming silence and magic clips from longer videos add to the toolkit. Multiple languages are supported.

item.title: Transkriptor
item.description:
Transkriptor turns speech into text. Users upload files, record in the app, or connect meeting platforms, and receive a transcript with timestamps and speaker labels that can be edited and exported. Subtitles and translations are supported.

Features include meeting bots that join calls, AI summaries, and a chat assistant to ask questions about a recording. It serves students, journalists, researchers, and businesses.

Transkriptor has a free trial and paid plans by hours. Accuracy depends on audio quality, and sensitive recordings need privacy checks. Alternatives include Otter.ai, Trint, Descript, Fireflies, and Whisper-based tools. Transkriptor suits people transcribing interviews and meetings.

item.title: Trint
item.description:
Trint speeds up working with recordings. Users upload interviews, press conferences, or footage and get transcripts that link to the audio, so editing the text is easy to verify. Teams can search across an archive, highlight quotes, and build stories from selections.

The platform supports many languages, translation, and subtitles, and offers collaboration for newsrooms with permissions and shared workspaces. AI features create summaries and help extract key moments.

Trint is paid, with plans by features and seats. Accuracy depends on audio quality. Alternatives include Otter.ai, Descript, Transkriptor, Verbit, and Rev. Trint suits media teams that work with large volumes of recorded content.

item.title: Verbit
item.description:
Verbit blends machine and human work. AI produces a first draft of the transcript, and professional editors review and correct it, which yields higher accuracy than automatic transcription alone. Services include captioning for live events, court reporting, and transcripts of recorded media.

Education is a big market: universities use Verbit to caption lectures and meet accessibility requirements. Its platform integrates with video tools and learning systems, and the company has acquired several transcription and captioning firms.

item.title: AssemblyAI
item.description:
AssemblyAI is infrastructure for apps that need to understand speech. A developer sends audio from a call, meeting, podcast, or video, and the API returns an accurate transcript with word-level timestamps. It supports pre-recorded files and real-time streaming, so it can power live captions and voice assistants as well as batch transcription. Customers use it to build call analytics, meeting note takers, media search, and compliance tools.

Beyond transcription, a layer of speech understanding turns text into structured data. It can separate speakers, summarize a conversation, detect topics, and score sentiment. Guardrails features redact personal information and filter sensitive content before the data goes anywhere else. An LLM Gateway lets developers pass transcripts to language models for tasks like extracting action items, and a voice agent API supports speech-to-speech applications.

item.title: Deepgram
item.description:
Deepgram sells speech AI to developers. Its speech-to-text API transcribes audio in real time or from recordings, and it is designed for accuracy at low latency and low cost, which matters for call centers, meeting tools, and voice assistants that process large volumes. Features include speaker labeling, punctuation, keyword boosting, and support for many languages, and models can be customized to a company’s vocabulary.

The platform has widened to cover the whole voice stack. A text-to-speech product generates natural voices with low latency, and a voice agent API combines speech recognition, a language model, and speech synthesis into a single service for building conversational agents that can hold phone calls. Enterprises can run Deepgram in their own cloud or on-premises when data cannot leave their control.

item.title: Hedy AI
item.description:
Hedy AI takes a different role from notetakers that summarize afterward. It listens during a call or conversation and shows prompts in the moment: a suggested answer, a question to ask, or a reminder of context. The goal is to help the user perform better while the conversation is happening.

After the meeting, it produces transcripts and summaries and can store notes for future sessions. People use it for sales calls, interviews, negotiations, and learning situations. It can run alongside video calls or in person on a phone or computer.

item.title: Mumble AI
item.description:
Mumble AI is built around talking instead of typing. Users dictate ideas or record meetings, and the app turns speech into structured notes, highlighting tasks and decisions. Apps on Mac and iPhone sync so a thought captured on the go is waiting at the desk.

It targets busy professionals who think out loud: managers between meetings, founders, and consultants. Features include summaries, task extraction, and searchable archives.

Independent information about Mumble AI is limited, so check where audio is processed and stored. It has a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include Otter, Granola, Superwhisper, Voicenotes, and Apple Notes with transcription. Mumble AI suits people who prefer to capture notes by voice.

item.title: Read AI
item.description:
Read AI began as a meeting analytics tool. It joins calls on Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, and other platforms, then produces a transcript, summary, action items, and chapters. What set it apart was measurement: reports on engagement, speaker time, and sentiment, giving meeting organizers a sense of how a conversation went and who participated.

The product has expanded across communication channels. Read AI can summarize emails and messages, and its search and Q&A features answer questions across meetings, email, and chat, so you can ask what was decided about a project or what a client said last month. Integrations send summaries to Slack, Notion, Salesforce, and HubSpot. A copilot can prepare you for upcoming meetings by pulling relevant history.

item.title: Voicetype AI
item.description:
Voicetype AI lets people speak instead of type. A user holds a hotkey, speaks, and the text appears in the active app, with punctuation and formatting handled automatically. It works across email, documents, chat, and code editors.

AI cleans up filler words and false starts, and supports many languages. Custom dictionaries help with names and jargon. Dictation can speed up writing for people who think out loud.

Voicetype AI has a free tier and paid plans. Independent information is limited, so check privacy and where audio is processed. Alternatives include Wispr Flow, Superwhisper, Dragon, Apple dictation, and Talon. Voicetype AI suits people who want voice typing everywhere.

item.title: Zoom AI Companion
item.description: AI Companion is the assistant built into Zoom’s meeting, chat, phone, and document tools. Its most used feature is the meeting summary: it listens to the call, produces a transcript, and writes up the main points and action items, which it can share with attendees right after the meeting ends. If you join late, it can catch you up on what was said. It can also answer questions about a meeting in progress, such as what was decided on a topic a few minutes ago.
